name: Gelatin / bone broth

image.caption: Amino Acid Composition in Gelatin chart

lead: Gelatin and bone broth are collagen-derived foods. Gelatin is made by partially breaking down animal collagen, mostly from pork skin, bones and cattle hides, and bone broth is a long-simmered stock in which collagen converts to gelatin. Wellness and looksmaxxing communities eat them to support skin, hair and joints.

Proponents reason that eating collagen-derived amino acids supplies building blocks for skin and hair. Regulators and reference sources report that a cause-and-effect link between ingested collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance has not been established, and no studies of appearance outcomes were found.

paras: People drink bone broth as a daily or regular warm drink or cooking base, or eat gelatin as dessert or stirred into drinks. It is used as part of an overall diet alongside other protein. Users who report skin or hair changes describe weeks to months.

Gelatin is a protein food and is generally treated as low risk, though some people are allergic to gelatin in injected drugs. It is not suitable for vegetarian, halal or kosher practice depending on the source.

chain: Building blocks for skin and hair
angle.text: Fans eat gelatin and bone broth because collagen-derived amino acids are thought to supply building blocks for skin and hair. Reference sources report that a link between ingested collagen and joint maintenance has not been established, and no appearance studies were found.

lead: Gelatin and bone broth are collagen-derived foods. Gelatin is made by partially breaking down animal collagen, mostly from pork skin, bones and cattle hides, and gels in water.[1] Bone broth is a long-simmered stock of animal bones and connective tissue, in which collagen converts to gelatin and thickens the liquid.[2]

In looksmaxxing and wellness circles they are eaten as inexpensive dietary sources of collagen's amino acids, with the aim of supporting skin firmness, hair and joints. One looksmax.org guide recommends gelatin as a low-cost collagen supplement for skin, and a poster in that thread reported noticing changes from it.[3] The chain proponents describe runs from amino acids such as glycine and proline to the connective tissue that gives skin its structure, and to joint comfort that lets people keep training.

Research has looked at collagen and gelatin in several settings: a trial of vitamin C-enriched gelatin before intermittent exercise measured collagen synthesis,[4] and a systematic review of collagen peptides with exercise reported benefits mainly for joint function and pain, with some improvements in body composition and recovery.[5] The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that a cause-and-effect relationship between collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance had not been established.[1][6]
infobox: Animal collagen, converted to gelatin by simmering
About 98 to 99% protein, not a complete protein[1]
Bone broth popularised by the early 2010s[2]

paras: Stock made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables is a traditional cooking base; the connective tissue releases collagen that becomes gelatin and gives the liquid body.[2] Gelatin itself is used in desserts, confectionery, capsules and cosmetics, and can be made at home by boiling cartilage-rich bones or cuts.[1]

Dry gelatin is nearly all protein, but it lacks tryptophan and is low in several other amino acids; glycine, proline and hydroxyproline make up roughly half of its amino acids.[1] Collagen and gelatin are used across food, pharmaceutical and cosmetic industries, and fish-derived versions exist for safety and religious reasons.[7][8]

Gelatin-like dishes appear in a 10th-century Arabic cookbook and a 14th-century French recipe, and extraction methods improved in the 1700s and 1800s.[1] The bone broth health trend took off by the early 2010s, with the 2014 book Nourishing Broth credited with promoting claims about its nutrient density.[2]

A looksmax.org thread titled as a guide to collagen supplements calls gelatin the best and cheapest option and points to a systematic review of oral collagen in 11 studies and 805 participants, covering skin aging, xerosis and cellulite, as supporting skin benefits.[3] On T Nation, members mention beef gelatin used to thicken protein-rich meals and bone broth as a food during illness or low-carb eating, without appearance claims.[9][10][11]

Proponents link collagen foods to skin, hair and joint health. The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that a cause-and-effect relationship between collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance had not been established.[1][6] Reference summaries note that hydrolysed collagen is used in creams as a conditioner and moisturiser, which concerns topical use rather than eating.[1][6]

A 2025 review of bone broth's components examined amino acids and minerals in the context of gut barrier function and inflammation, drawing on animal and human studies.[12] Regulators consider the disease-transmission risk from bovine bone gelatin very low under standard processing.[1]

Gelatin is a protein food, but allergic reactions to gelatin in injected drugs and vaccines are documented, and a review discusses how to prevent such reactions.[13] Alpha-gal syndrome, a delayed allergy to mammalian meat, is a separate condition managed by avoiding mammalian products.[14] Gelatin sources also matter for vegetarian, halal and kosher practice.

Studies of dietary gelatin or broth for appearance outcomes were not found. Related human research covers collagen products in exercise and joint settings. In a randomised study, vitamin C-enriched gelatin taken before intermittent activity was tested for effects on collagen synthesis.[4] A systematic review of 15 randomised trials of collagen peptides with exercise found the most benefit for joint function and pain, with certain improvements in body composition, strength and recovery.[5] A trial in active adults examined collagen peptides for function, pain and physical and mental outcomes.[15] These concern collagen peptides or gelatin supplements, not broth.
